answer: so the cash flow statement has three sections. cash flow from operations starts with net income, adds back non cash items like depreciation and stock comp, and then adjusts for changes in operating assets and liabilities like receivables, inventory and payables. cash flow from investing covers the long term side of the business, so capex on property and equipment, acquisitions of other companies, and buying or selling investments. cash flow from financing is how the company raises and returns capital, so issuing or repaying debt, paying dividends, and issuing or repurchasing shares. now the current versus long term rule of thumb is not perfect because there are exceptions. deferred revenue can be a long term liability but it still sits in operations. short term investments are current assets but they go in investing. and the revolver is a current liability but it goes in financing.

so a decrease in prepaid expenses means we are now recognizing an expense that we already paid cash for earlier. on the income statement, expenses go up by 100, so pre tax income goes down by 100, and with a 40 percent tax rate net income falls by 60. on the cash flow statement, we start with net income down 60, then a decrease in prepaid expenses, which is an asset, is a source of cash so we add back 100. that gives us a net cash increase of 40. on the balance sheet, cash is up 40 and prepaid is down 100, so total assets fall by 60. on the other side, retained earnings fall by 60 through net income, so both sides drop by 60 and it balances. the intuition is that the cash already left earlier, and now we just get the tax savings of 40 from the expense. if prepaid went up instead, we paid cash in advance, so cash goes down, prepaid goes up, and nothing hits the income statement.

the revolver is a short term borrowing facility, basically like a company credit card, so on the balance sheet it is a current liability. the reason it still goes in cash flow from financing is that the cash flow statement sections are organized by what the activity is about, not by the balance sheet classification. cash flow from operations is about the core business, things like receivables, inventory and payables. the revolver is not part of that, it is a way the company finances itself. when the company draws on it or pays it down, it is changing how the business is funded, which is a financing decision. so the revolver is one of the exceptions to the current versus long term rule of thumb, along with things like deferred revenue and short term investments, and it goes in financing.

so the revolver, i think of it like a credit card for a company, and actually my uncle runs a small landscaping business and he has a line of credit with his bank that he draws on in the winter when there is less revenue, and then pays down in the spring, so that is basically a revolver. so a revolver is short term borrowing, it is a current liability on the balance sheet, because it is supposed to be repaid within a year, or at least the amount that is drawn. but then on the cash flow statement it goes in cash flow from financing, not operations. and the reason is that the cash flow statement is organized by what the item is related to and not just whether it is current or long term. so operations is things that relate to the core business, like selling products and collecting from customers, and paying suppliers, and working capital like inventory. financing is about how the company raises money to fund itself, so debt, equity, dividends. and the revolver is borrowing money, it is about funding the business, so it belongs in financing even though it is current. this is one of the exceptions people talk about, the other ones i remember are deferred revenue, which could be long term but is in operations, and short term investments, which are current assets but go in investing. i also heard that in an lbo model the revolver is the first thing you draw on if you have a cash shortfall, and it is cheaper than the term loans usually, and has a commitment fee on the undrawn part, which is a fun detail. but anyway the main point for this question is it is financing because it is how the company funds itself. and also, thinking about it more, in a three statement model you would often have the revolver draw automatically if cash goes below a minimum balance, so the model would be circular because of the interest, and that is why people use a circularity toggle, which my professor made us do in a lab.

yes, under accrual accounting a company records revenue when it is earned, not when the cash shows up, as long as collection is reasonably assured. the most common case is a credit sale, where a company delivers a product to a customer on 30 day terms. revenue is recognized at delivery and the company books accounts receivable, and the cash comes a month later. another example is a subscription or service contract where the company bills in arrears, so it has already delivered the service for the period, recognizes the revenue, and collects later. a third example is a long term contract, like a construction project or enterprise software implementation, where revenue is recognized over time as the work is performed, based on percent completion or milestones, even though the customer pays in installments. in all of these the key idea is that revenue follows performance, so the income statement matches what was earned, and the gap between revenue and cash shows up as a receivable or unbilled revenue on the balance sheet.

okay so this is really about accrual accounting versus cash accounting, and i remember my intermediate accounting professor spending like three weeks on revenue recognition, she loved it, and she always said that enron was the example of what happens when you push it too far, which is a whole other story. so under accrual accounting you record revenue when it is earned and collection is reasonably assured, not when cash comes in. a super common example is a credit sale. so say a company sells equipment to a customer on net 30 terms. they deliver it, they record revenue right then, and they put accounts receivable on the balance sheet, and then 30 days later the customer pays and receivables goes down and cash goes up. my cousin owns a small print shop and he does exactly that with his business clients, he sends the invoice and waits forever for people to pay, which stresses him out a lot. another example is subscription services. so like a software company that bills customers after the month is over, they delivered the service during the month, so they recognize that revenue even though the invoice has not been paid. and then there are long term contracts, like construction or something like building a ship, where you recognize revenue over the period of the project, based on percent complete, or milestones. and the customer might pay in chunks, or at the end. there is also the new asc 606 standard which changed a lot of this, with the five step model, identify the contract, performance obligations, transaction price, allocate and recognize when you satisfy the obligation. so the main idea is that you match the revenue to when the work is done and not to the cash, and that is why you see receivables, and sometimes unbilled revenue on the balance sheet. and also on the cash flow statement you have to adjust for the receivables increase in operations, which is why net income and cash flow from operations are different. so yeah that is when a company records revenue before getting cash. and just one more example that i think is interesting, which is when companies report revenue from a bundle of products, like a phone with a service plan, and then they have to split the revenue between the pieces and recognize each one when it is delivered. also there is the opposite situation, where you get cash before revenue, that is deferred revenue, like a magazine subscription that you pay for a year in advance, and the company records a liability and recognizes the revenue slowly. i bring it up because it is the mirror image, and between the two you can see that accrual accounting is about timing. my aunt works in the billing department of a hospital and she says the insurance companies pay them months after the patients are treated, and they still count the revenue when the treatment happens, but they have to estimate how much they will actually collect, which is why there is an allowance for doubtful accounts. so yeah, that is how collection being reasonably assured fits in, because if you doubt that you will get paid you either do not record it or you reserve against it, and i think that is a really important point because it is what keeps companies honest.

i would start with the market, since lenders ultimately decide how much and what kind of debt a deal can get. first i would look at debt comps, so recent lbos of similar companies in the same industry and size, and see what total debt to ebitda and senior debt to ebitda they got, and at what pricing. that usually gives me a range, for example four times senior and five and a half times total. second, i would check the company itself against that range. i would look at interest coverage, ebitda divided by cash interest, usually wanting at least two times, and fixed charge coverage, and run the model to see whether free cash flow can pay down debt over five to seven years. stable, recurring cash flows can support more leverage than cyclical ones. for tranches, it follows from the same research. typically a revolver and term loan a or b on the senior secured side, then senior notes or high yield, and maybe second lien or mezzanine for the junior layer, each sized to market appetite from banks, clos and credit funds. then equity is the plug for whatever is left.

this is unusual, because it implies that ebitda is smaller than ebit, which means d and a is negative. here is the math. enterprise value is the same in both multiples. if ev over ebit is 3 times and ev over ebitda is 4 times, then ebit has to be bigger than ebitda, since the same ev divided by a smaller number gives the bigger multiple. and ebitda equals ebit plus depreciation and amortization, so ebitda can only be smaller if d and a is a negative number. normally d and a is a positive add back, so ebit is always less than ebitda. a negative d and a could happen if there was a reversal of a prior impairment, amortization of negative goodwill, or some other one time credit running through the d and a line. so i would conclude it is probably an accounting anomaly or a non recurring item rather than a normal operating business, and i would want to look at the financials and adjust the numbers before using these multiples in any valuation.

the company with debt has the lower wacc, at least up to a point. debt is cheaper than equity for two reasons. lenders have a senior claim so they demand a lower return than shareholders, and interest is tax deductible, so the after tax cost of debt is even lower, which is the interest tax shield. so when you replace some expensive equity with cheaper after tax debt, the weighted average falls. now for the follow up, the wacc starts to rise when leverage gets too high. as debt piles up, lenders worry about default so the cost of debt rises. and equity holders face more financial risk, their beta goes up, so the cost of equity rises too. at some point the increase in both costs outweighs the benefit of the tax shield from adding another dollar of debt, and wacc turns up. that is the trade off theory of capital structure, where there is an optimal debt level that minimizes wacc, and past that point the levered company can have a higher wacc than the all equity one, because of financial distress costs.

the fundamental difference is how predictable the cash flows are. an apple tree produces fruit every year for many years, and you can estimate the harvest and the price of apples, so the cash flows look like an annuity. you could value it with a discounted cash flow using a fairly low discount rate, because there is little uncertainty. a race horse is far more speculative. its value depends on how many races it wins, prize money, and eventually breeding or stud fees, and all of those are uncertain. the other difference is duration and stability. a horse has a short and volatile earning period. it can get injured, underperform, or just age out of racing in a few years, and then the value drops. an apple tree gives steady returns for decades. so the tree is valued as a stable annuity, and the horse is more like an option, where there is a small chance of a huge payoff and a high chance of nothing, so it needs a much higher discount rate and a probability weighted approach.

so this is one of those things that confused me for a long time, honestly, and i had to ask my accounting tutor to explain it like three times. the reason you add back the whole non cash expense on the cash flow statement is that the expense lowered net income but no cash actually left the business. so say you buy a machine for a hundred thousand dollars, that is a cash outflow in investing, and then each year you depreciate it, which is just spreading the cost, there is no cash going out in those later years. so on the income statement, depreciation is an expense that reduces pre tax income. and because it is deductible, you pay lower taxes. so let us say the depreciation is 10 dollars and the tax rate is 40 percent. pre tax income is down 10, taxes are down 4, so net income is down 6. and then in the cash flow statement you start with net income, which is down 6, but you want to know actual cash, so you add back the full 10 since it was not cash. and you end up with cash up 4. and that 4 is the tax savings, the company paid 4 less in taxes in cash because of the depreciation deduction. now some people think you should add back the after tax number, 6, but if you did that you would get zero change in cash, and that would be saying the depreciation had no effect on taxes, which is not true. my friend in the finance club made that mistake in a mock interview, and the interviewer, who was an actual analyst, pointed it out. i think about it like the depreciation is a tax shield, you get a real benefit, and the tax shield is why it is not a total wash. also this is why capital intensive companies like utilities or airlines have big depreciation and the cash flow is higher than the net income, which is something i noticed when i looked at delta's statements for a class project.

so this is a good question because it kind of challenges what people assume. the standard answer is that the real purchase price is closer to the purchase equity value and not the enterprise value, and the reason is how debt and cash get handled in a deal. so, in most acquisitions, the buyer is not just writing a check for the debt. what actually happens is it usually refinances the seller's existing debt and replaces it with new debt in the same amount, so it is not paying extra for the debt, it just swaps lenders. my dad refinanced our house last year and it is kind of like that, same loan amount just a different bank and a lower rate. so since the debt is replaced, the real extra cost is not the debt. then for cash, if the seller has excess cash, it is usually distributed to the shareholders before the deal closes, or if it stays on the balance sheet then the acquirer gets it when the deal closes, and that is economically equivalent, because it is either paid out or it comes over with the company. so you could say the real price is something like purchase equity value plus the transaction and financing fees, minus the excess cash of the seller. i read about this in the breaking into wall street guide and also on a forum, and some people say it is a bit of a technicality. and of course there can be variations, like if the debt has change of control provisions and has to be paid off at a premium, or if the cash is trapped overseas and the buyer cannot use it easily. in those cases it could be different. but the base case is the equity value. also this is why enterprise value is used for comparing across companies, since it is capital structure neutral, but it is not what the acquirer actually pays out of pocket. i think that is the main idea.
